extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, researchers, and policymakers interested in media economics and journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes economic criteria and forces that determine which information becomes news and how market incentives shape news content across media. Includes historical observations and policy recommendations to improve the public value of news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story selection determinants
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a story appears in print, on television, or on the Internet depends on who is interested, its value to advertisers, the costs of assembling the details, and competitors’ products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list is presented as the primary economic determinants of news selection; each factor (audience interest, advertiser value, reporting costs, competitive offerings) influences editors' decisions about which items become news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketability/profitability criterion for news
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is transformed into news when there is an identifiable market for it and when it seems likely to yield a profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton frames news as a commodity: market demand and expected profitability are core filters converting raw information into news items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-targeted content via marketing decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: News is presented to specific audiences, depending on marketing decisions, leading outlets to tailor stories to demographic preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: evening news broadcasts aiming to retain young female viewers ran stories aligned with their interests, demonstrating demographic targeting alters story selection and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser influence and shift toward soft/celebrity news
rubrics_metrics.description: The value to advertisers and market incentives encourage shifts from hard political news toward more soft news about entertainers, celebrity profiles, and product hype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic logic explains phenomena often criticized as media bias or 'fluff' coverage; these are not necessarily editorial failings but responses to commercial incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and competition shaping news content (structural factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cable competition, deregulation, and ownership changes encourage content shifts (e.g., from political hard news to softer entertainment-oriented news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural market changes alter outlet incentives and audience fragmentation, producing systematic shifts in the news menu across time periods (supported by historical analysis 1969–1998).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonpartisan reporting as a historical norm
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis shows how nonpartisan reporting became the norm (newspapers 1870–1900), although partisan elements can reemerge under different market incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as a descriptive standard: nonpartisanship arose historically under particular economic conditions; deviations often reflect changed incentives rather than pure editorial choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for conflict/adversarial framing over exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: News tends to brim with conflict and an adversarial pose that substitutes for hard information, as outlets use conflict to attract audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton documents audience preferences (e.g., younger viewers prefer more conflict and less exposition) and shows how conflict-focused presentation serves market-driven attention-capture goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation: lower costs of access to government information
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamilton calls for lower costs of access to government information to improve the supply of hard news and public-interest reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing barriers to public records and data can lower reporting costs and thereby increase the feasibility and profitability of hard news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation: greater role for nonprofit funding of journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: He recommends a greater role for nonprofits in funding journalism to counteract market incentives that underproduce public-interest reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonprofit funding is presented as a corrective to purely commercial incentives, supporting content (investigative, civic) that may not be immediately profitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation: develop norms that stress hard news reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamilton calls for the development of journalistic norms that emphasize hard news reporting to counterbalance commercial pressures toward softer content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm-building is framed as a societal and professional response that complements structural and funding interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation: define digital and Internet property rights to encourage news flow
rubrics_metrics.description: He advocates defining digital and Internet property rights to encourage the flow of news in online environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifying rights and business models in digital contexts is suggested as a means to preserve incentives for news production and distribution on the Internet.
